explanation: An evaluation starts with a task and a definition of success. Collect representative cases, establish a baseline, and keep some examples untouched while improving the system.
A model judge can help review outputs, but may share biases with the model being evaluated. Human review and deterministic checks remain useful.
mechanism: An evaluation starts with the task and definition of success. A rubric breaks quality into observable criteria; a representative dataset includes common, difficult, and missing-information cases. A baseline shows whether the new system improves on a simpler alternative.

Held-out examples reduce tuning bias. Blind review hides system identity to reduce preference effects. Regression tests detect lost capabilities after changes. Human review can assess nuance; model judges can scale review but may favor particular wording or miss factual errors. Validate judges against independent decisions.
example: You evaluate a course tutor on beginner questions.
The rubric checks correctness, understandable vocabulary, realistic examples, and whether it admits missing information. Reviewers see answers without model names.
A verbose model scores lower when it invents facts, even if its explanations sound polished.
use: Create the evaluation before optimizing prompts or selecting a model. Include failure cases that matter to actual users.
caution: Testing only questions used during development measures familiarity more than generalization.
question: Why include questions with no answer in the supplied documents?
answer: To test abstention and evidence boundaries. A system that always answers can appear helpful while inventing unsupported information.
title: Designing evaluations
scope: Task definitions, rubrics, representative datasets, baseline comparisons, blind review, held-out cases, regressions, human evaluation, and model-as-judge limitations.

explanation: Accuracy counts correct predictions overall. Precision asks how many positive predictions were right; recall asks how many real positives were found. The right balance depends on consequences.
For serving, averages can hide slow outliers. Latency percentiles and cost per successful task can tell you more than raw token speed or cost per request.
mechanism: Accuracy counts overall correct decisions. Precision asks how many flagged cases are truly positive; recall asks how many true positives were found. F1 combines precision and recall into one summary, which can hide the tradeoff. Ranking metrics evaluate ordering rather than only labels.

Calibration compares confidence with observed correctness. Perplexity measures predictive fit to token sequences, not broad usefulness. Latency percentiles reveal slow tails: a good average can hide long waits. Cost per successful task includes failures and retries, not just the price of one call.
example: Of 100 tickets, 10 are urgent. A classifier flags 8, of which 6 are truly urgent.
Its precision is 6 out of 8, while recall is 6 out of 10. Four urgent cases were missed, and two ordinary tickets were escalated.
Whether that tradeoff is acceptable depends on the cost of missed urgency versus extra review.
use: Choose metrics from the decision's consequences. Report sample sizes, relevant subgroups, and variability rather than a single flattering score.
caution: A classifier that labels all 100 tickets non-urgent is 90% accurate here but finds none of the urgent cases.
question: Why might p95 response latency matter more than the mean for a chat product?
answer: It exposes delays experienced by slower requests that an average can conceal, helping assess whether users frequently encounter unacceptable waits.
title: Reading metrics
scope: Accuracy, precision/recall, F1, ranking quality, calibration, perplexity, latency percentiles, cost per successful task, and uncertainty—all interpreted through examples, not formulas.

explanation: Trace a failure through the pipeline: source data, retrieval, prompt assembly, model, tool execution, and interface. Locate the first incorrect step before changing the system.
An ablation removes or changes one component to test its contribution. Changing many things at once can improve results while leaving you unsure why.
mechanism: An AI application is a pipeline, so failures can originate in data, retrieval, prompts, the model, tools, or the execution environment. Traces record the sequence of events and relevant inputs/outputs. A failure taxonomy groups recurring problems so fixes target causes rather than symptoms.

An ablation removes or changes one component to test its contribution. Controlled experiments vary one important factor while keeping others stable. Record revisions and settings; seeds do not fully eliminate nondeterminism. Protect sensitive information in logs while retaining enough evidence to reproduce failures.
example: A support assistant gives the wrong warranty answer.
The trace shows the correct document was retrieved but omitted during context truncation. Switching to a larger model would not directly repair that assembly bug.
The team preserves the relevant exception and adds a regression case for long requests.
use: Follow the evidence from user input to final outcome. Fix the earliest incorrect stage that explains the failure.
caution: An attractive answer is not an end-to-end trace, and a model upgrade should not substitute for diagnosing broken tooling.
question: How would you test whether reranking improves your system?
answer: Compare the same held-out queries with and without reranking, keeping the rest fixed, and measure both retrieved evidence and final answer quality.
title: Debugging the whole system
scope: Traces, data quality, retrieval, prompt, model, tools, environment, one-variable experiments, ablations, reproducibility, seed limits, and failure taxonomies.

explanation: A paper's contribution depends on the problem, baseline, dataset, evaluation, and resource budget. Read limitations and ablations, not just the headline score.
Contamination occurs when evaluation material leaks into training or tuning. A leaderboard improvement may not transfer to your workload. Seek reproducible evidence.
mechanism: Start a paper by identifying its question, claimed contribution, and comparison baseline. Inspect datasets, train/test separation, compute budget, and how success is measured. Ablations test which components contribute to results; limitations describe where evidence is weak or applicability narrow.

Contamination occurs when evaluation content influences training or development. Leaderboard overfitting happens when repeated tuning targets a benchmark rather than broader needs. Reproducibility requires enough artifacts and settings to check results. A proposed explanation may be plausible without being directly demonstrated.
example: A paper reports a large improvement on one benchmark.
Its new system also uses more inference attempts and a different evaluation prompt.
You separate the method's contribution from added compute and test whether the improvement holds on your own representative tasks.
use: Read tables with their experimental conditions. Look for independent replications and failures before generalizing a result.
caution: State-of-the-art is always relative to a benchmark, date, comparison set, and evaluation procedure.
question: What would an ablation that removes retrieval help establish?
answer: Whether retrieval contributed to the measured result under those conditions. It would not by itself prove the same gain for every dataset or deployment.
title: Reading papers and benchmarks
scope: Research question, baseline, dataset, method, compute, ablations, limitations, benchmark contamination, leaderboard overfitting, reproducibility, and separating evidence from speculation.
